Moreover, using synthetic data, we show that neglecting the observational effects in the model biases the inferred parameters by up to 2.5 sigma and also underestimates their uncertainties. Finally, we show that varying the number of foreground modes removed and the range of scales included changes the inferred parameters by less than 0.5 sigma. These results demonstrate the robustness of our pipeline in modelling HI intensity mapping data, and set the foundation for future cosmological inference with intensity mapping using MeerKLASS and SKAO.

title: Elliptic master integrals and the one-loop cosmological wavefunction
summary: Loop corrections to the cosmological wavefunction involve similar integrals to those required for scattering amplitudes. For the one-loop triangle of a conformally coupled scalar, the master integrals are elliptic, and so the triangle wavefunction coefficient was expected to be elliptic as well. Using a bootstrap approach, we compute this triangle coefficient exactly and show that it is not: the elliptic periods cancel, and the flat-space wavefunction coefficient is a combination of dilogarithms. The cancellation occurs because the residue of the loop integrand on the elliptic sector is a flat-space amplitude, rational in the loop momentum. The one-loop box, by contrast, is not polylogarithmic, even with a single external leg at each site. Its threshold discontinuity involves elliptic integrals, which we also give in closed form. For regular-tetrahedron momenta the periods of a K3 surface enter its loop integrand.

title: Testing Extended Exponential Infrared Teleparallel Gravity with CMB, DESI, and PantheonPlus
summary: We place cosmological constraints on an extended exponential infrared (EExpIR) $f(T)$ teleparallel gravity model using current observational datasets. The extension is characterized by an additional parameter, $b$, which governs the late-time cosmological dynamics. Owing to the existence of two solution branches, phase-space analysis is employed to select the cosmological branch and to establish an appropriate prior range for the new parameter. In this framework, the torsion sector acts as an effective dark-energy component, exhibiting a smooth evolution from a quintessence-like phase to a phantom regime, while recovering the standard cosmological behavior at early times. To constrain the model parameters, we combine early-Universe observations from Planck, ACT, and SPT measurements of the CMB with late-time probes from DESI BAO and PantheonPlus Type Ia supernovae. Using the full dataset, including the SH0ES calibration, we obtain $b=0.573^{+0.016}_{-0.060}$ and $H_0=70.67^{+0.31}_{-0.35}~{\rm km\,s^{-1}\,Mpc^{-1}}$ at 68\% CL. Model comparison based on Bayesian evidence reveals that the EExpIR $f(T)$ and the $Λ$CDM models are statistically indistinguishable when only CMB data are considered, whereas the inclusion of the full cosmological dataset with SH0ES leads to a weak preference in favor of $Λ$CDM.

title: Kinematic methods of spiral nature identification: limitations and applicability
summary: The nature of spiral arms in galaxies remains debated, with several competing formation scenarios, including density waves, kinematic spirals, dynamic spirals, and recurrent modes, that are difficult to distinguish observationally. We tested two kinematic methods - the phase reversal method and the velocity harmonic dominance method - using toy models and mock data from TNG50 simulations. For bar resonances, the phase reversal method is strongly orientation-dependent and yields reliable corotation estimates only when the bar is aligned with the disc minor axis. For spiral arms, the phase reversal method does not always yield reliable results and should be used in tondem with another kinematic method. The velocity harmonic dominance method is more robust: it distinguishes between density wave, kinematic, and dynamic spiral patterns, although it still shows some sensitivity to orientation. Uncertainties in the rotation curve do not strongly affect its results. We also apply both methods to the observed grand-design spiral galaxy NGC3938 as an illustrative example; the results suggest the presence of multiple spiral modes, consistent with the recurrent modes scenario and this interpretation relies on different indirect evidence. Based on our findings, we propose a strategy for classifying spiral structure in observed galaxies that combines multiple independent tests. Applying this analysis to an extended sample will allow us to validate its predictive power and to investigate the diversity of spiral formation scenarios.

title: Atmospheric Parameter Determination of RR Lyrae Stars With Mephisto Multi-band Photometry
summary: Phase-resolved atmospheric parameters of pulsating stars, including RR Lyrae stars and Cepheids, are essential for studying stellar structure and pulsation physics and for establishing accurate stellar benchmarks for Galactic structure and assembly history. We present a photometric framework that simultaneously infers Teff, log g, and [Fe/H] from Mephisto multi-epoch, multi-band (u, v, g, r, i, z) photometry. A supervised neural-network forward model is built by training on synthetic colors derived from theoretical stellar atmosphere models. It reproduces the synthetic colors to a precision of 0.01 per cent. The model is applied to observed multi-epoch colors to derive phase-dependent atmospheric parameters. We apply the method to six RRab and four RRc stars in three globular clusters observed with Mephisto. We find typical per-phase uncertainties of about 62 K in effective temperature (Teff), 0.10 dex in surface gravity (log g), and 0.16 dex in metallicity ([Fe/H]). Repeated measurements across the pulsation cycle reduce the typical formal uncertainty of the final [Fe/H] estimates to roughly 0.03 dex. A sensitivity analysis indicates that the five Mephisto colors provide distinct and complementary constraints on the three stellar atmospheric parameters: (u-v) provides robust constraints on log g, (v-g) is informative for estimating [Fe/H], and (u-v), (v-g), (g-r), (r-i), and (i-z) all provide information on Teff. The results demonstrate that Mephisto multi-epoch, multi-band photometry can deliver precise, cost-effective phase-resolved atmospheric parameters for RR Lyrae stars, offering an efficient way to construct large samples of stellar benchmarks for studies of stellar pulsation physics and Galactic structure and evolution.

title: Identifying narrow-band mutual coupling resonances in SKA-low stations using frequency-independent current basis functions
summary: Mutual coupling between closely spaced elements in aperture arrays introduces narrow-band spectral features in the Embedded Element Patterns (EEPs), threatening measurements of the 21-cm power spectrum with instruments such as SKA-low. We detail a method to identify such features through the construction of frequency-independent current basis functions, utilising a singular value decomposition of frequency-dependent basis functions. We demonstrate the method on a three-element linear array and full pseudo-random station of SKA log-periodic antennas and examine the current power induced by mutual coupling. For the pseudo-random layout station we note many narrow-band resonance features, including strong resonances at 50.8~MHz and 83.6~MHz, where the coupled power on the passive antennas can approach or exceed that of the excited antenna. Simulated delay power spectra for the SKA-low core show that observing in frequency bands including resonance features causes large foreground leakage within the delay power spectra, obscuring the EoR window. For the pseudo-random layout station with SKALA4.0 we identify two significant frequency bands from 59.2--76.2~MHz and 84.2--103.3~MHz which are free of contamination from current resonances, preserving the EoR window in these frequency ranges.

title: Benchmarking Quantum Neural Networks Developed for MBHB Coalescence in the Context of LISA Space Mission
summary: Machine learning (ML) techniques are increasingly explored to analyse gravitational wave (GW) data expected from the Laser Interferometer Space Antenna (LISA). At the same time, advances in quantum computing have stimulated interest in quantum machine learning as a potential alternative to conventional approaches. We investigate the applicability of quantum, hybrid quantum-classical, and classical ML models to two tasks relevant for LISA observations of massive black hole binaries: GW signal detection and merger prediction. Using the Sangria dataset from the LISA Data Challenge, we benchmark several quantum architectures, including variational quantum classifiers (VQCs), post VQC hybrid models, quantum kernel methods, data reuploading classifiers, and quantum long short-term memory (QLSTM) networks, against classical support vector machines, multilayer perceptrons, recurrent neural networks, and LSTM networks. The models are trained on labelled data derived from the Sangria training dataset and evaluated on the corresponding blind dataset. For signal detection, several quantum models match or outperform classical baselines. In particular, the best performing hybrid post VQC architecture correctly identifies all signal samples in the blind dataset, while the standard VQC and data reuploading classifier achieve competitive detection rates. For merger detection and coalescence time estimation, however, the standard VQC emerges as the most reliable model, successfully localising all detected merger events with the lowest localisation errors. We further analyse the trade-offs between predictive performance, model complexity, and quantum circuit resources. Our results indicate that, although no universal quantum advantage is observed, selected quantum models can provide practical benefits for specific GW analysis tasks and represent promising candidates for future LISA data analysis pipelines.

title: The Korean Space Telescope (KST): A Dedicated Space Observatory for the Dark Universe
summary: The Korean Space Telescope (KST) is a next-generation 1.4-meter wide-field space observatory, a dedicated probe of the dark sector. Its single instrument provides diffraction-limited visible imaging (~0.15 arcsec in the optical) together with simultaneous near-infrared (R ~ 100) slitless spectrophotometry, so that every detected source is observed in the NIR by the survey itself, with spectral information delivered at a resolution set by its brightness (full R ~ 100 typing at the bright end, synthetic medium-band or broadband photometry below it) and with no separate follow-up, a capability decisive for time-domain science. With it, KST addresses the three outstanding questions of dark physics in concert: the dynamics of dark energy, the nature of dark matter, and gravitational-wave dark sirens as independent cosmological rulers. KST combines measurements of expansion and structure growth to test dark-energy models. A two-tiered "Wedding Cake" strategy (2,000 deg^2 Wide plus 10 deg^2 cluster-targeted Deep Survey) combines weak lensing, baryon acoustic oscillations, and a near-infrared-standardized Type Ia supernova Hubble diagram to constrain dark energy at its pivot redshift (sigma(w_p) ~ 0.03); maps dark matter from cluster cores to galactic substructure to test cold dark matter against warm and self-interacting alternatives; and builds a deep near-infrared host catalog for a distance-ladder-independent H_0 from dark sirens. The same data yield a Legacy Science portfolio (galaxy evolution, active galactic nuclei, exoplanets, and the Milky Way) at no additional observing cost. As Korea's first dedicated astrophysics space mission, KST occupies a niche complementary to the Vera C. Rubin Observatory, Euclid, and Roman.

title: Tabular Foundation Models Dramatically Outperform Bespoke Photometric Redshift Estimators
summary: Estimating galaxy redshifts (a proxy for distance) from imaging data alone, also known as photometric redshifts (photo-$z$'s), is essential for studies of extragalactic astrophysics and cosmology. However, data-driven estimators rely on spectroscopic training datasets, which are scarce and systematically biased toward bright and easily observed galaxies. In this work, we show that tabular foundation models (TFMs), whose synthetic pretraining amounts to a learned prior over regression problems, can outperform bespoke estimators using only in-context learning. Evaluating on a widely used benchmark dataset, we find that TFMs predicting full probability distributions in a single forward pass systematically outperform bespoke estimators across both representative and biased training data regimes, matching or exceeding baselines trained on over $40{,}000$ galaxies with just $1{,}000$ training context examples. We also show that the TFM advantage is largest when little to no calibration data are available, and that it persists even when the bespoke baselines are supplemented with up to $10{,}000$ representative calibration spectra. This shows that TFMs offer a sample-efficient framework for upcoming imaging-only astronomical surveys, where observational selection bias can be mitigated simply by including a small representative calibration sample in context.

title: Energy-flux noise induced by imperfections of the Gaussian beam in the Li-Baker HFGW detector
summary: This paper investigates the energy-flux noise induced by imperfections of the Gaussian beam (GB) in the Li-Baker high-frequency gravitational wave (HFGW) detector. Modeling these imperfections with higher-order Laguerre-Gaussian (LG) beams, we analytically derive the resulting noise-to-signal ratio for both co- and cross-polarized $\mathrm{LG}_{nl}$ modes. It is found that higher-order co-polarized LG beams generate no tangential energy-flux noise at the optimal detection plane ($φ=π/2$ or $3π/2$), whereas higher-order cross-polarized LG beams introduce non-negligible noise. Specifically, for an individual higher-order cross-polarized $\mathrm{LG}_{nl}$ mode under our representative parameters, maintaining the noise-to-signal ratio below unity typically requires the power fraction to satisfy $σ_{nl}<10^{-46}$, with the $\mathrm{LG}_{01}$ mode imposing the most stringent constraint of $σ_{01}<6.0\times10^{-49}$. Monte Carlo simulations suggest that the total power fraction $σ_{\mathrm{total}}$ of multiple higher-order cross-polarized $\mathrm{LG}_{nl}$ modes needs to remain below $10^{-49}$. Consequently, we propose employing a polarization filter to retain only the co-polarized component of the GB adopted in the practical experiment, thereby suppressing the noise while preserving signal integrity. These results provide theoretical guidance for noise control in the Li-Baker HFGW detector.

title: Search for Cosmic Rays in GRANDProto300
summary: GRANDProto300 is a prototype array of the GRAND experiment, designed to validate the technique of autonomous radio-detection of astroparticles by detecting cosmic rays with energies between 10$^{17} - 10^{18.5}$ eV. This observation will further enable the study of the Galactic-to-extragalactic source transition region. Between November 2024 and June 2025, 46 antennas were operational, and since July 2025, 63 antennas have been collecting data stably. We present here our cosmic-ray search pipeline, that involves several filtering steps: (1) exclusion of clustered (in time and space) noise events, (2) polarization cut, (3) zenith arrival cut, and (4) delay in expected trigger cut. The efficiency is evaluated on the latest batch of data from July 2025 to October 2025. Additionally, we present an identification layer that is being developed: a CNN-based algorithm to discriminate between noise and cosmic-ray signals, using signal traces. We present the accuracy of our model, trained both on simulations and on real cosmic-ray signal datasets.

title: Efficient GLS map-making and assessment of $1/f$ noise impact for future CMB satellite missions
summary: Time-correlated $1/f$ noise is a major source of large-scale contamination in measurements of the polarized cosmic microwave background (CMB) that can limit sensitivity to primordial $B$ modes. Generalized least-squares (GLS) map-making is optimal for stationary Gaussian noise when its covariance is known, but practical implementations rely on approximations to make the computation tractable. In particular, approximating the noise covariance as circulant enables efficient map-making using fast Fourier transform, but introduces artificial edge effects when applied to finite data chunks. We introduce STITCH (STatistical Inpainting for Timeline CHunks), a preprocessing method that mitigates these effects by extending time-ordered data chunks with synthetic samples that make the extended timelines statistically consistent with the assumed circulant noise model. They can then be processed with standard circulant GLS solvers, preserving their computational efficiency while reducing residuals associated with chunk boundaries. Simulations show that STITCH substantially suppresses these edge effects, bringing the resulting noise power spectra close to those obtained when the circulant approximation holds. We demonstrate negligible impact of our procedure on the recovered signal, such as $E\to B$ leakage, even at large scales. Finally, we investigate how temporal $1/f$ noise projects onto angular scales for representative LiteBIRD-, \emph{Planck}-, and PICO-like scanning strategies. Using noise simulations spanning a range of temporal noise parameters, we fit an effective model to the resulting angular noise spectra. These results provide an empirical characterization of the temporal-to-angular noise mapping for the configurations studied and a basis for further investigations of correlated noise in future CMB polarization missions.

title: A deep learning approach to member identification and mass estimation in galaxy clusters
summary: Accurate dynamical mass estimates of galaxy clusters are essential for studies of cluster formation and evolution and for cosmological applications. However, interloper galaxies, which are not gravitationally bound to the cluster but are incorrectly identified as members, can bias dynamical mass measurements and increase uncertainties. We developed a probabilistic deep-learning framework for cluster member identification and dynamical mass estimation and tested sensitivity to cluster miscentring and radially dependent incompleteness in controlled mock experiments. We used mock galaxy cluster catalogues to train a two-stage model. A long short-term memory (LSTM) network assigns membership probabilities to galaxies arranged by projected phase-space proximity. These probabilities construct membership-weighted projected phase-space density maps, from which a Bayesian neural network (BNN) infers cluster masses and predictive uncertainties. The LSTM membership probabilities are well calibrated and form an isoprobability envelope in projected phase space, with the $\langle p_{\rm mem}\rangle = 0.5$ contour broadly tracing the empirical member--interloper transition. A threshold of $p_{\rm th} = 0.5$ balances member completeness and purity, with high completeness within $R_{\rm proj} < r_{200}$. Membership weighting lowers the residual scatter of the fiducial BNN mass estimator, $\mathrm{BNN}^{\mathrm{Mem}}_{\mathrm{2D}}$, to $σ_ε= 0.120$, a 19.5% reduction relative to the unweighted baseline, although predictive uncertainties are not uniformly calibrated across BNN models. Using the brightest cluster galaxy rather than the gravitational centre lowers the median inferred mass by up to 47.6%, with larger reductions at larger centring offsets. By contrast, removing 40% of eligible non-central galaxies within $r_{200}$ lowers it by 6.1% relative to complete catalogues.

title: Running cosmological constant in light of recent CMB-BAO data
summary: We revisit single-field slow-roll inflation driven by a running cosmological constant, i.e. a cosmological constant receiving a logarithmic radiative correction, in light of the latest CMB-BAO data. The relative radiative correction $δ$ is treated as a free parameter of the model and allowed to be positive or negative. For positive $δ$, the predictions interpolate between a logarithmic regime and a linear inflation one. Compatibility with CMB-only data is confined to a narrow stripe near the $2σ$ border where $δ$ is relatively large. On the other hand, the predictions fit easily within the constraints including BAO data in a wide range of parameters. For negative $δ$, the slow-roll approximation breaks down at small field values and the predictions are excluded by data. However, once the effective mass contribution inside the logarithmic correction is taken into account, the negative $δ$ potential develops a local maximum and behaves like a hilltop model, achieving compatibility with CMB-only data, while agreement with CMB-BAO data is possible only at $2σ$.

title: A morpho-kinematic view of the Necklace nebula
summary: We present a morpho-kinematic study of the Necklace Nebula based on spatially resolved spectroscopic observations and 3D modeling performed with the SHAPE software. The nebula is characterized by an equatorial disrupted ring accompanied by bipolar outflows. The geometry and velocity field of these different components are derived from the comparison between observed and synthetic images and position-velocity diagrams. The best model successfully reproduces the main morphological and kinematic features of the nebula, allowing us to constrain its 3D structure. We confirm that the disrupted ring is tilted about 60° from the plane of the sky, but the bipolar outflows are inclined by 46° with respect to the line of sight. This situation might indicate that the bipolar structures are not simple extensions of the equatorial ring, but instead correspond to a distinct mass-ejection event. The slight misalignment between these two components suggests either precession of the ejection axis, a temporal change in the dominant mass-loss geometry, or a misalignment in the magnetic field. Given that the Necklace Nebula hosts a close binary central star and is a well-established post-common envelope planetary nebula, our results support a scenario in which binary interaction plays a central role in shaping its morphology, even before the common envelope phase.

title: Probabilistic Stellar Mass and Radius Estimation with Bayesian Hierarchical Stacking
summary: Accurate stellar parameters are essential for the characterisation of exoplanets, yet most host stars lack direct measurements of mass and radius. We aim to predict stellar masses and radii from commonly available observables and to quantify uncertainties and systematic effects in a way that is consistent with stellar observations. By not relying on a single model, we aim to obtain more robust predictive distributions and reduce sensitivity to model misspecification and outliers. We develop a Bayesian machine-learning framework that combines three probabilistic models through Bayesian hierarchical stacking (BHS): a Bayesian additive regression tree model, a two-process heteroscedastic sparse Gaussian process, and a hierarchical Bayesian neural network. The method propagates measurement uncertainties, accounts for correlations among inputs, and aggregates model variance into final predictive distributions. On a held-out test set the method attains a mean absolute relative difference (MARD) of 3.5% for mass and 2.1% for radius, improving on empirical-relation-based methods and standard machine-learning baselines. For 44 Kepler LEGACY stars, the BHS masses differ from estimates obtained with the BAyesian STellar Algorithm (BASTA) by a MARD of 4.8%, compared with 8.5% between the empirical relations and BASTA. Applied to about 2400 exoplanet host stars, the predictions differ from literature values by a MARD of 2.7% in both mass and radius. Residual analysis reveals mild underestimation for cool dwarfs, consistent with sparse training coverage, and positive offsets near the main-sequence turn-off that may reflect priors in isochrone-based catalogues. Internal consistency with g = GM/R^2 is greater for the BHS predictions, with a scatter in Delta log g lower by a factor of three than that of the literature values.

title: Simulating and Characterizing Non-Gaussian Small-Scale Polarized Emission
summary: Galactic foregrounds present a major challenge for cosmic microwave background (CMB) cosmology as their amplitudes exceed the target primordial $B$-mode signal. While small-scale interstellar medium (ISM) emission is expected to be highly complex, current foreground simulations cannot reproduce the filamentary, non-Gaussian features of ISM structure in a stochastic way. To address this gap, we introduce a framework for generating stochastic small-scale foreground emission, using polarized synchrotron observations as an example use case. This method is capable of producing many independent realizations that additionally inherit morphological information from large angular scales. The underlying structural complexity incorporates anisotropic, multifractal, and advected non-Gaussian features that are tunable with a small number of parameters that carry physical interpretations. Because standard power spectra do not describe the complex phase coherence required for the structural complexity, we evaluate the synthetic fields using higher-order statistics, demonstrating that the Minkowski functionals and structure functions partially capture varying degrees of non-Gaussianity. This work lays the necessary foundation for new foreground simulation suites with stochastic realizations of possible non-Gaussian structure.

title: Validating an X-ray-based method for identifying Fermi blazars
summary:
Context. Blazars are the main population of active galactic nuclei (AGNs) detected in gamma rays by Fermi. However, around 34% of Fermi sources remain unidentified, partly due to their large positional uncertainties, motivating multiwavelength methods to identify possible counterparts.
  Aims. We evaluate a method proposed to identify BL Lacertae (BL Lac) candidates among unidentified Fermi sources based on their X-ray properties, using Swift-XRT observations.
  Methods. We examined published optical spectra for an initial sample of 148 X-ray-selected candidates. We found 71 sources with spectra spatially consistent with the proposed associations and reassessed their classifications using standard blazar criteria. We then compared these classifications with the method's initial predictions.
  Results. Of the 71 proposed counterparts, 80.28% are classified as BL Lac objects and 87.32% as possible gamma-ray-emitting AGNs, supporting the effectiveness of the X-ray-based selection. We also identify four Seyfert galaxies, suggesting that the method is sensitive to this class despite its rarity among gamma-ray emitters.
  Conclusions. Our results show that X-ray observations are effective for selecting BL Lac candidates among unidentified Fermi sources and support future spectroscopic follow-up campaigns. The high fraction of BL Lacs and AGNs suggests that blazars may account for a substantial part of the unidentified gamma-ray population. The Seyfert identifications also raise questions about the origin of high-energy emission in AGNs not typically associated with relativistic jets, highlighting the need for further multiwavelength observations.

title: Combining Multiple Incomplete Astronomical Surveys to Estimate Galaxy Flux Distributions
summary: In astrophysics, the distributions of fluxes or intensities of populations of sources provide insight into the structure and evolution of the universe. We propose a science-driven hierarchical Bayesian framework to estimate the X-ray flux distribution of a population of galaxies. The distribution is parameterized via a broken power law model, formulated as a mixture of Pareto distributions, and is fit using data from a combination of non-representative X-ray and optical surveys. Because fainter sources are less likely to be detected, astronomical surveys suffer from incompleteness at the low-intensity end, and dedicated survey simulations are used to study the resulting missing-data pattern and determine the form of corrections. We introduce a methodology to combine data from two (or more) surveys with different incompleteness functions. This allows us to leverage deeper surveys (e.g., optical) to more fully characterize the X-ray log(N)-log(S) (where fewer sources are detected). We take advantage of a well-calibrated characterization of the missing-data pattern, particularly in X-ray surveys, to make incompleteness corrections for sources that are not detected in either survey. The proposed model is validated using a simulation study designed to mimic the Chandra Deep Field South (CDF-S), demonstrating accurate recovery of the flux distribution even under high proportions of systematic incompleteness. Finally, we apply our proposed method to data from the CDF-S.

title: Primordial Gravitational Waves in Loop Quantum Cosmology: Regularization Ambiguities and Initial State Dependence
summary: We compute the primordial tensor power spectrum in standard loop quantum cosmology and in the modified models mLQC-I and mLQC-II, evolving the tensor perturbations across the bounce in the hybrid and dressed metric prescriptions with a Starobinsky potential. In mLQC-I, the emergent de Sitter contracting branch requires the use of dedicated initial states. We use de Sitter mode function in the dressed metric approach and a Hankel-function solution in the hybrid approach. For inflationary e-foldings $N_e = 60$ and $65$, the pivot-scale tensor-to-scalar ratio agrees with the value of standard inflation with this potential. The scale-dependent ratio $r(k)=\mathcal{P}_T/\mathcal{P}_S$ cancels effects common to the two sectors and separates features that are independent of the initial state from those that depend on it. It varies slowly in the scale-invariant regime and oscillates around $r_\star$ at smaller $k$. The oscillations next to the scale-invariant regime do not depend on the adiabatic order, unlike the peaks and spikes at lower $k$. For a given initial state, the regularization dependence survives in the infrared, where long-wavelength modes retain a record of the bounce and of the pre-bounce branch. We propagate the normalized spectra to the CMB $B$-mode spectrum and discuss observational prospects.

title: Are Black Hole and Cosmological Horizon Thermodynamics Necessarily Inequivalent?
summary: It has recently been argued that cosmological horizon thermodynamics and black hole thermodynamics are generically inequivalent in any consistent, UV complete theory of quantum gravity, where it was suggested that this could be falsified by the identification of a counterexample. This conjecture was motivated in part by noting that cosmological horizons do not incorporate many of the convenient features found in the black holes described by string theory. In this work, we consider as a toy model a universe with a single non-rotating black hole and a positive cosmological constant. We work in the Nariai limit where the mass of the black hole is taken to its maximum possible value, and where we also assert that the quantum field theory living on this background is strictly parity invariant. In the semi-classical regime where we neglect instability of the exact Nariai equilibrium under quantum fluctuations, we find that the observer cannot readily distinguish the physics in the neighborhood of the black hole horizon from the physics in the neighborhood of the cosmological horizon. This does not prove that the two are generically equivalent in any universe, though it does suggest that they cannot be entirely unrelated in general. We propose that any consistent theory of quantum gravity that aims to describe black holes in a universe with a positive cosmological constant should provide a related microscopic origin for the leading semiclassical cosmological entropy and black hole entropy in the neighborhood of the particular limit considered here.

title: Cosmic birefringence tomography with radio galaxies I: Testing birefringence solutions to the CMB-BAO tension
summary: We present an independent test of cosmic birefringence induced by axionlike particles (ALPs) at low redshift using radio galaxies. We focus on models that can alleviate the mild tension between recent baryon acoustic oscillation (BAO) measurements and observations of the cosmic microwave background (CMB). This tension can be explained by a large cosmic birefringence rotation angle generated during the reionization epoch. Such a large rotation can arise if the recent isotropic cosmic birefringence measurements are subject to an $nπ$ phase ambiguity, with $n\in\mathbb{Z}$, or if cold dark matter injects energy into ALPs. We constrain these two scenarios by fitting the cosmic birefringence angles estimated from the jet morphologies and polarization angles of radio galaxies obtained by Battye, Jackson & Browne (2026). For the $nπ$ model, the radio-galaxy data exclude $|n|\geq 1$ at more than $2σ$ for $\log_{10}(m_φ/{\rm eV})\lesssim -30.7$. For the energy injection model, the data are consistent with no energy injection, but with a slight relative preference for a nonzero energy injection compared to the no-injection case. Since our samples are limited to $\sim 3000$ and there could still be several astrophysical uncertainties and statistical fluctuations, further exploration of tomographic cosmic birefringence using a large number of low-redshift radio galaxies is important for independent tests of cosmic birefringence.

title: Hot off the Stacks: X-rays in Romulus25, Part I - Comparisons to Observations from eRosita
summary: Recent observations from the from Spectrum Roentgen Gamma (SRG)/eROSITA all-sky survey data have helped to illuminate the hot circumgalactic medium (CGM) around galaxies at Milky Way-masses and above. In our study, we explore the hot X-ray emitting (T \textgreater 10$^6$ K) component of the CGM in over 750 galaxies from the Romulus25 cosmological simulation (Tremmel et al. 2017) between 10.0 < log(M$_*/M_{\odot}$) < 11.5. We forward-model soft X-ray [0.5 - 2.0] keV observations of our simulated galaxies using pyXSIM and SIXTE to measure the X-ray surface brightness (SB) profiles of the hot CGM. We then compare the average X-ray surface brightness profiles of six stellar-mass selected sub-samples to compare to the observational results from Chadayammuri et al. (2022a) and Zhang et al. 2024a. Broadly, we find that our stacked SB profiles are too bright compared to observations from Chadayammuri et al. (2022a) and Zhang et al.(2024a) particularly in the inner CGM. Additionally, we calculate the X-ray luminosity (L$_χ$) of the hot CGM for each galaxy and compare the average L$_χ$ across stellar mass to observations from Zhang et al. (2024b) as well as measurements from the EAGLE, TNG, SIMBA simulations. Across stellar mass, the average L$_χ$ of galaxies from Romulus25 are brighter than observations except at the lower, Milky Way-mass end where we are in relative agreement with both observations and most other simulations. We also consider a zero-metallicity emission model, because Romulus25 does not have metal-line cooling, finding the average L$_χ$ decreases by nearly an order-of-magnitude, which better matches observations particularly in the Milky Way-mass regime.

title: SuperCrude EoS: A Simple, Analytical, and Reasonably Accurate Equation of State for Astrophysical Fluid Dynamics
summary: We present SuperCrude, a vastly simplified astrophysical equation of state that captures the most important physics needed for explosive astrophysics, but using compact, physically-motivated analytical approximations rather than precise interpolated data tables. We present a number of code tests demonstrating the performance of SuperCrude in a wide range of parameter space. In large regions of parameter space, SuperCrude is precisely accurate to within the accuracy level of helmeos. For some regions (especially where degeneracy, gas, and radiation are comparable) SuperCrude has errors in its effective adiabatic index on the order of a few percent. The solver's estimate of the temperature is less accurate, on the order of tens of percent. Because the solver is analytic, SuperCrude is designed in such a way to guarantee exact thermodynamic consistency. We incorporate SuperCrude into some hydrodynamic and astrophysical test problems, including the thermonuclear explosion of a white dwarf star. When coupled with a stiff nuclear network, SuperCrude does not achieve the same nucleosynthetic yields as helmeos, motivating future work to improve the temperature accuracy further.

title: Environmental Quenching of Satellite Galaxies out to z~0.4 with GAMA and DEVILS
summary: While numerous studies have shown that satellite galaxies experience declining star formation rates after infall, direct comparisons across different surveys and redshifts are complicated by varying sample selections, environmental metrics, and techniques used to derive galaxy properties. In this work, we select satellite galaxies from the highly complete Galaxy and Mass Assembly (GAMA) Survey and the Deep Extragalactic VIsible Legacy Survey (DEVILS) to investigate environmental quenching out to z~0.4. These surveys derive galaxy properties and environments in a consistent manner, minimizing systematic biases and enabling a robust comparison across redshift. Using projected phase space as a proxy for infall time, we quantify the evolution of the quenched fraction and trace how satellites evolve relative to the star-forming main sequence (SFMS). We find consistent trends between GAMA and DEVILS, with satellites exhibiting a steady decline in star formation relative to the SFMS at a rate of ~0.14 dex/Gyr following infall. Extending this analysis to include visual morphology, we find similar declining trends for both early- and late-type systems. Overall, we find no significant redshift evolution between GAMA and DEVILS, indicating that group and cluster environments have a comparable impact on the star formation activity of satellite galaxies over the past ~4.5 Gyr.

title: The coupled evolution of nuclear star clusters and intermediate-mass black holes in a dwarf-galaxy merger
summary: Nuclear star clusters (NSCs) and intermediate-mass black holes (IMBHs) are expected to coexist in low-mass galaxies and might together facilitate the coalescence and growth of IMBHs. We simulate an equal-mass, gas-rich dwarf-galaxy merger in which each progenitor hosts a $10^3\,\rm M_\odot$ IMBH embedded in a $10^6\,\rm M_\odot$ NSC to study their co-evolution. The simulation model combines the multiphase interstellar medium and fully sampled initial stellar mass function of GRIFFIN at $4\,\rm M_\odot$ gas resolution with the regularised post-Newtonian black hole dynamics of KETJU. Black holes are modelled as accreting sink particles without feedback. Without NSCs, $10^3$-$10^4\,\rm M_\odot$ IMBHs sink only to separations of $50$-$200\,\rm pc$ and capture no gas. With NSCs, the clusters coalesce within ${\sim} 500\,\rm Myr$, the IMBHs form a binary within a few Myr, and scattering of mainly old NSC stars drives them to merger ${\sim} 340\,\rm Myr$ later. The NSCs also promote gas capture, growing the black holes to $1.1\times10^5$ and $4.1\times10^4\,\rm M_\odot$. Gas capture is suppressed during the merger-induced starburst by stellar feedback and the motion of the NSCs relative to the gas, and proceeds in brief supernova-regulated episodes once the NSCs have settled in the centre. Scattering by the IMBH binary and the merger recoil of ${\sim} 175\,\rm km\,s^{-1}$, which removes the remnant from the NSC but not from the galaxy, leave a larger, rotating NSC with a flat core. The stellar tidal disruption rate rises towards coalescence, and the merger is detectable with LISA out to high redshift. NSCs thus remove the delivery and hardening bottlenecks of IMBH mergers in low-mass galaxies.

title: Probing the local primordial non-Gaussianity with clustering of FRB dispersion measure and galaxies
summary: We forecast the sensitivity of a joint fast radio burst (FRB) and galaxy survey to local primordial non-Gaussianity using the full $3\times2$-point statistic: the angular dispersion-measure (DM) auto-spectrum, the DM-galaxy cross-spectrum, and the galaxy auto-spectrum. Local primordial non-Gaussianity imprints a scale-dependent bias on both the free-electron field probed by FRB dispersion measures and the galaxy field. Hence, all three spectra carry information on the local non-Gaussianity amplitude $f_{\rm NL}$. Adopting a DESI-like luminous-red-galaxy sample and an FRB population over 35% of the sky, we forecast $σ(f_{\rm NL}) \simeq 5$ for both $N_{\rm FRB} = 10^4$ and $10^5$ at fixed Planck 2018 cosmology, marginalised over three astrophysical bias parameters $(b_e^0, z_{\rm fb}, b_g^{\rm amp})$. The $f_{\rm NL}$ constraint is robust to marginalising over the six $Λ$CDM parameters $(ω_b, ω_{\rm cdm}, h, A_s, n_s, τ)$ with Planck priors. At these sample sizes, the galaxy auto-spectrum sets the constraint, while the DM sector's contribution grows with the burst count and becomes decisive for the larger samples anticipated in the SKA era, reaching $σ(f_{\rm NL}) \simeq 2$ at $10^7$ bursts.

title: The nature of the Norma arm as a bar-driven star-forming shock front
summary: The Milky Way is commonly depicted as having four major spiral arms, including the Norma-Outer arm, and a central stellar bar whose properties remain debated. Masers associated with young high-mass stars have been used to trace a segment of the "Norma arm" extending from one end of the Galaxy's central stellar bar. Recent work suggests that these masers may reside along a spiral arm or occupy the dominant x1 stellar orbits that give the bar its shape. We now use a new generation of N-body, hydrodynamic simulations to argue that these million-year old masers instead trace the Galactic bar's Quadrant I shock front or, equivalently, its dust lane. This implies that the bar dust-lane is star-forming, shedding new light on our understanding of star formation processes in the Milky Way. By associating the masers with the simulated shock front, we determine the bar's parameters to be: a ~ 4.3 +/- 0.2 kpc, b ~ 2.3 +/- 0.2 kpc, phi = 20 (+5/-2) deg, Omega_p <~ 40 km s^-1 kpc^-1, representing the bar's semi-major and semi-minor half-lengths, inclination angle and pattern speed, respectively. This raises questions about the Milky Way's spiral structure and suggests that the Galactic bar is long, slow and star-forming.

title: PyMsOfa 2.0: A Pure-Python Implementation of the IAU Standards of Fundamental Astronomy Service
summary: Astrometric calculations require authoritative algorithms so that every result is correct and reproducible. The Standards of Fundamental Astronomy (SOFA) service of the International Astronomical Union (IAU) provides such algorithms, officially released only in Fortran 77 and ANSI C. In an earlier paper we presented the first version of PyMsOfa, a Python package wrapping the SOFA C library. Here we present PyMsOfa 2.0, which re-implements the complete SOFA library in pure Python with NumPy. All 247 official SOFA routines are ported directly to Python, requiring no compilation of any external C library and running identically on Linux, Windows, and macOS. The routines operate on NumPy arrays, so arguments can be processed in batch, which is convenient for survey pipelines and Monte Carlo simulations. The package also provides an extension module with validated models not yet part of the official SOFA release, such as the improved precession--nutation model IAU 2006$_{J_2}$/2000A$_{R26}$. The reimplementation reproduces the official SOFA algorithms: all constants, series, and coefficients are taken unchanged from the SOFA source files, and routine names differ only by the pym prefix. We verify every routine against the official SOFA C release: most reproduce the C results to machine precision, the remainder within the accuracy tolerance stated in the SOFA documentation. The package has been applied to Gaia astrometric reduction and used in astrometric studies of the Closeby Habitable Exoplanet Survey (CHES) mission, and is available through PyPI, GitHub, and Zenodo.

title: The Radio Neutrino Observatory in Greenland (RNO-G) - System Design and Instrumentation
summary: The Radio Neutrino Observatory in Greenland (RNO-G) is designed to measure cosmic neutrinos in the EeV range through an array of radio antennas detecting nanosecond-long radio flashes. In this contribution, the RNO-G electronic system is outlined, illustrating how signals are measured from the antennas to the recorded pulses. We present new instrumentation developments, focusing on electric melters to install LPDA antennas into the Greenlandic ice sheet. The new system will simplify deployment and reduce positioning uncertainty to $\pm$2cm (x/y) and $\pm$1°(rotational). We report on field tests from the RNO-G site at Summit Station.

title: Detection of HNCOH+ in the interstellar medium
summary: Only five out of the $\sim$350 molecules detected in the interstellar medium (ISM) carry the isocyanate functional group (NCO), the essential substructure of peptide bonds in proteins. Among them are isocyanic acid (HNCO) and its most stable N-protonated isomer H$_2$NCO$^+$. Previous studies have predicted that the O-protonated isomer HNCOH$^+$ should be present in the ISM; yet this species has remained elusive. We search for the metastable HNCOH$^+$ towards the Galactic Center molecular cloud G+0.693-0.027, where H$_2$NCO$^+$ has already been detected. We use an ultra-deep broadband spectral survey carried out towards G+0.693-0.027 with the Yebes 40-m, IRAM 30-m and APEX telescopes covering nearly 150 GHz of bandwidth between 31 and 275 GHz. We report the first detection of HNCOH$^+$ in the ISM with a column density of $N$ = (9.9 $\pm$ 0.5)$\times$10$^{12}$ cm$^{-2}$, which corresponds to a molecular abundance relative to H$_2$ of (7.3$^{+1.3} _{-1.0}$)$\times$10$^{-11}$. With the measured H$_2$NCO$^+$ column density of $N$ = (2.6 $\pm$ 0.3) $\times 10^{12}$ cm$^{-2}$, this yields a HNCOH$^+$/H$_2$NCO$^+$ ratio of 3.8$^{+0.5} _{-0.4}$. This result is consistent with recent kinetic calculations that favour the formation of HNCOH$^+$ over H$_2$NCO$^+$. The detection of HNCOH$^+$ in the ISM broadens the inventory of molecules known to contain the isocyanate functional group and reinforces recent works showing that isomer abundances in the ISM do not necessarily correlate with thermodynamic stability.

title: The Peculiar Astrometric Behaviour and Radio Structure of the Quasar 1524-136 Revealed with Very Long Baseline Interferometry
summary: According to astrometric very long baseline interferometry (VLBI) observations accurate to sub-milliarcsecond levels, the radio quasar 1524-136 (J1526-1351) exhibited an exceptionally large shift, more than 0.1", between the 1990s and 2010s. This luminous quasar is known for its extended (~0.4"), highly asymmetric and non-collinear jet structure. Here we analyse historical VLBI astrometric and imaging data, as well as Gaia optical astrometric information, to find the cause of the sudden apparent change in the position. At the X band (~8.4 GHz frequency), where radio positions are conventionally measured, the core region brightened substantially relative to the hotspot at the end of the northern jet. As a result, the brightness peak shifted from the hotspot to the core, causing the VLBI position to shift accordingly. Similar changes could affect the astrometric positions of other radio sources. A better understanding of the astrophysical reasons behind them is important for maintaining the stability of the VLBI-based celestial reference frame.

title: The Pointing Error Due To Laser Propagation in Space Plasma for TianQin Gravitational Wave Detection
summary: TianQin, a space-borne gravitational wave observatory, is designed to detect gravitational-wave signals via laser interferometry. As the inhomogeneous space plasma surrounds the inter-satellite laser links, the propagation of the laser in space plasma can introduce pointing error noise. In this work, we quantitatively assess the effect of plasma on the pointing accuracy of TQ's inter-satellite laser links. We employ a magnetohydrodynamic model to simulate the plasma distribution around the TQ orbit for different orbital orientations. Using the fourth-order Runge-Kutta method to conduct the ray-tracing calculations over a TQ orbital cycle under a solar wind dynamic pressure close to the 23-year average, we find that the plasma-induced laser deflection angle and pointing eccentricity are on the order of $10^{-20} \ \mathrm{rad}$ and picometers, respectively. These values are significantly lower than TQ's requirements. Our results demonstrate that the impact of space plasma on TQ's pointing error is negligible in moderate space weather conditions, indicating a positive outlook for the TQ mission.

title: Four-hundred Very Metal-poor Stars Studied with LAMOST and Subaru. IV. Heavy Element Enhanced Stars
summary: We perform a homogeneous analysis of 82 heavy-element-enhanced metal-poor stars from the\\ LAMOST/Subaru sample, including 64 $r$-process-enhanced stars, 2 limited-$r$ stars, and 16 stars exhibiting significant or moderate carbon enhancement (comprising 9 $s$-process-enhanced, 2 $r$-process-enhanced, 2 $r$/$s$, and 3 $r$+$s$ stars). Systematic differences in $\mathrm{[X/Eu]}$ between $r$-I and $r$-II stars, together with their distinct dynamical properties, suggest that $r$-II stars likely formed in low-mass dwarf galaxies where contamination from additional nucleosynthetic channels was minimal. We have also discovered a number of peculiar objects. We identify an extremely metal-poor $r$-II star, J1158+0734 ($\mathrm{[Fe/H]}$ = -2.93), whose enhanced Zn abundance ($\mathrm{[Zn/Fe]}$ = +0.67) is best explained by yields from a high-energy, massive core-collapse supernova. The surface abundances of $s$-process-enhanced stars exhibit pronounced dispersion, consistent with enrichment from AGB progenitors with diverse properties. Notably, one star, J2256+0215, reveals compelling evidence for additional evolutionary mixing, as indicated by its unusually low carbon abundance ($\mathrm{[C/Fe]}$ = +0.08) and extremely low $^{12}$C/$^{13}$C ratio of 2.33. Additionally, we identify 3 $r$+$s$ stars whose abundance patterns reveal combined contributions from both the $r$- and $s$-processes. We further propose a modified diagnostic scheme for the identification of CEMP-$r$+$s$ stars, defined as: -0.2 $\leqslant$ $\mathrm{[La/Nd]}$ $\leqslant$ 0.2 and -0.5 $\leqslant$ $\mathrm{[Eu/Nd]}$ $\leqslant$ 0.0.

title: The Conditional CMB Visibility of High-Redshift X-Ray Cavities in Galaxy clusters
summary: At high redshift, the cosmic microwave background (CMB) both cools relativistic leptons and provides seed photons for inverse-Compton (IC) X-ray emission. These two effects link the particle content of a bubble directly to the soft X-ray depression used to identify a cavity. We derive a physical criterion connecting lepton cooling, bubble volume, enthalpy evolution, and 0.5--2 keV X-ray visibility, while separating intrinsic filling of the X-ray depression from detector-dependent cavity recovery. For uncooled electron populations described by a power law with spectral index $s=2.5$, minimum Lorentz factor $100\leqγ_{\min}\leq1000$, and maximum Lorentz factor $γ_{\max}=10^5$, the measured atmosphere of the testbed high-redshift cluster SPT-CL J2215$-$3537 requires 0.6--1.2\% of the pressure in radiating leptons to fill the soft-band deficit. Across the full tested ranges of $s$, $γ_{\min}$, and atmospheric properties, the required fraction is 0.2--3.7\%. Complete loss of this component reduces the enthalpy by less than 3\% relative to an otherwise identical adiabatic bubble at the same pressure. A low-cutoff control with $γ_{\min}=10$ and $s=3$ instead requires 18.9\%, identifying the poorly constrained low-energy spectrum as the main physical uncertainty. For a fixed atmosphere and spectrum, the required fraction scales as $(1+z)^{-4}$. The declining-pressure tracks show that the X-ray deficit can cross the adopted detection threshold while the enthalpy deficit remains below 0.4\%; the time of this transition depends on the assumed pressure history. Thus, high-redshift cavity visibility depends on both the surrounding atmosphere and the pressure-carrying particle spectrum. This criterion provides the physical basis for an instrument-specific recovery analysis.

title: Cosmological lensing as a jump process
summary: We develop a jump-process formalism for the probability density function (PDF) of gravitational lensing fields. In the Born approximation, each lens adds a jump to the convergence $κ$ and the two components of the shear, making lensing a jump process in redshift. For independent lenses, the joint PDF of the lensing fields obeys a compensated Kolmogorov-Feller equation, which we solve in closed form in Fourier space and extend to clustered lenses using their two-point correlation function. A Fourier-Hankel inversion then yields the joint PDF of $κ$ and the shear magnitude $γ$, from which the magnification PDF follows, including its high-magnification tail, without sampling noise. We use these PDFs to train an updated version of the FLUMEN emulator, which makes likelihood-based inference from the full magnification distribution feasible across cosmologies. To motivate such analyses, we estimate that samples of $10^4$ Roman supernovae, $10^5$ Rubin supernovae, 300 Einstein Telescope standard sirens, and 12 LISA standard sirens could constrain the matter fluctuation amplitude $σ_8$ respectively to 4.8\%, 5.1\%, 8.5\%, and 19\%, with the other cosmological parameters fixed.

title: Celia: Catalog Embeddings Learned from cosmologIcal simulAtions
summary: Cosmological hydrodynamical simulations connect observed galaxies to cosmology and the physics of galaxy formation. Each simulation is expensive, and different codes model galaxy formation in different ways. We present Celia (Catalog Embeddings Learned from cosmologIcal simulAtions), a self-supervised foundation model that maps catalogs of subhalos and their galaxy properties to an embedding vector for the purposes of compression and organization of astrophysical and large-scale structure information. Celia is pretrained without parameter labels on the IllustrisTNG, SIMBA and Astrid suites of CAMELS and their N-body counterparts, by reconstructing masked subhalo properties and predicting the representations of a teacher network. Simple linear models fitted to the embeddings recover $Ω_{\mathrm m}$ with $R^2=0.999$, and $σ_8$ and both supernova-feedback amplitudes with $R^2\geq0.97$, in all three suites. The embeddings translate well to out-of-distribution simulations such as Swift-EAGLE, a code that Celia never saw. A linear model fitted on the three training codes predicts its $Ω_{\mathrm m}$ with a correlation coefficient $r=0.985$, and linear models fitted on 20 labeled simulations reach $r\geq0.94$ for $Ω_{\mathrm m}$, $σ_8$ and a supernova-feedback amplitude. We decompose the variation among the simulations of each suite into principal components of the embedding, and simple power laws of the simulation parameters describe the leading components. Celia gives simulated galaxy catalogs a shared coordinate system for simulation-based inference, emulation, the comparison of galaxy-formation models, the detection of physical degeneracies and the discovery of new astrophysical probes.

title: What kinds of strong star--black-hole encounters in AGN disks occur, and how often?
summary: Disks surrounding active galactic nuclei contain many stars and black holes, which will inevitably encounter one another. The outcome of these encounters depends on how closely and how rapidly the bodies meet. Extending previous studies, we account for initial relative velocities seeded by stochastic effects in the disk; incorporate a strong-encounter cross-section accounting for single- and binary-mediated interactions computed via direct two-body (Hill) or three-body (isolated) interactions; and present a repeated-encounter model accounting both for energy loss due to stellar encounters as well as the SMBH tidal field. We convolve our encounter model with a parametric family of natal stellar and binary populations, focused on varying binary fraction and period distribution. In our fiducial disk model, even though single-single interactions supply most encounters, binary-mediated interactions supply 68% of collisions; most encounters are well-approximated as parabolic; and stochastically-driven relative velocities are comparatively substantial and driven by gravitational perturbations from disk fluctuations and neighboring bodies. Our tools are ready to use in downstream applications, including several easily-expressed semianalytic approximations to key interaction phenomena.

title: Cosmological axion-photon interactions with a nonminimal dark gauge sector
summary: We study the cosmological evolution of radiation and dark radiation with nonminimal axion-photon-dark photon couplings. The Chern-Simons-type axion-gauge field interactions between the dark and visible sectors can induce energy conversion between photons and dark photons as well as polarization rotation during the propagation of radiation, leading to CMB spectral distortions and cosmic birefringence. Using the observed CMB monopole spectrum, we constrain the photon-dark photon energy conversion fraction, which is determined by the coupling constants and the evolution of the axion field. We further show that the parity-odd mixing interaction $φF\tilde{B}$ can partially relax the constraints on the standard axion-photon coupling, $φF\tilde{F}$, derived from the current observational limits of the cosmic birefringence angle.

title: NORI: a GPU-accelerated code for simulating self-gravitating and self-interacting dark matter
summary: Self-interacting dark matter (SIDM) can form cores in dark matter haloes and later drive their gravothermal collapse, raising their central densities far above those of NFW haloes. Simulating this collapse is computationally demanding, requiring increasingly short time-steps and a large particle number to resolve the shrinking core. We present NORI, an $N$-body code that runs on CPUs and GPUs and simulates isolated self-gravitating systems with elastic, isotropic self-interactions using a Monte-Carlo method. To avoid MPI communication in the tree walks, each compute node in CPU mode, and each GPU or group of GPUs in GPU mode, holds a copy of all particles and its own Morton-ordered tree. A fixed evaluation order makes the results bitwise identical on CPUs and GPUs. Applying scattering events sequentially conserves the momentum and energy of each pair to round-off and allows multiple scatterings per particle per step. With global time-steps in both codes, NORI is several times faster on CPUs than our AREPO-2 implementation. One four-A100 GPU node is up to 60 times faster per time-step than AREPO-2 on a 112-core CPU node. For a full core-collapse simulation, where AREPO-2 uses individual time-steps, the speed-up is $\sim 30$ for the central density to reach $10^3$--$10^4$ times the NFW scale density, $ρ_{\rm s}$. We follow a halo with $10^8$ particles within $r_{200}$ to a central density of $10^4\,ρ_{\rm s}$. Within the limit of about $2\times10^9$ particles set by data replication, NORI provides an efficient tool for isolated SIDM simulations, including gravothermal collapse and cluster collisions.

title: Focal plane modal estimation of high-order wavefront drifts on coronagraphic testbeds
summary: The upcoming Habitable Worlds Observatory (HWO) requires precise wavefront stability over long observation periods to directly image Exo-Earths, which are 10 orders of magnitude dimmer than their host star. Dark zone maintenance (DZM) has been proposed as a focal plane high-order wavefront sensing and control (HOWFSC) strategy to mitigate thermal and mechanical instabilities that cause slow-evolving high-order wavefront drifts, which ultimately degrade contrast. Here we present a modal dark zone maintenance (MDZM) algorithm that uses an Extended Kalman Filter (EKF) to estimate the drifting wavefront modes in the basis of the deformable mirror (DM) actuators used for control. The estimator derives information across the entire focal plane from probe-pair images, addressing deficiencies of DZM, and directly obtains a DM command, eliminating the need for Electric Field Conjugation (EFC) and its regularization parameter. MDZM has been demonstrated in simulation and in hardware on the Decadal Survey Testbed (DST) at NASA JPL. These experiments have maintained a normalized intensity (NI) of $\sim 3 \times 10^{-10}$ for over 36 hours, and have reduced the gap to the photon-derived theoretical bounds compared to DZM. MDZM also provides an estimate of naturally occurring drift on the testbed, offering potential system identification capabilities. To evaluate the robustness of MDZM, a parameter scan is conducted on DST, spanning exposure times and drift rates. Additionally, realistic observing scenarios for HWO will involve broadband images with a 20% bandwidth, rather than the 2.5% narrowband images previously used in MDZM testbed demonstrations. Therefore, we tested MDZM in simulation using broadband sensing images with a 10% bandwidth, using the FALCO software package with a model based on DST, and compared its performance against MDZM runs using narrowband images.

title: Shock detection in meshless finite mass hydrodynamic schemes
summary: Shocks are prevalent in a multitude of astrophysical plasmas. They are essential in the dissipation of gravitational potential energy during structure formation, where they channel it into heat, turbulence, magnetic fields, and particle acceleration. Accurately capturing shocks in simulations of cosmological structure formation is a considerable challenge, due to the complexity of overlapping and colliding shocks, embedded in a medium experiencing complex shear flows. Fully Lagrangian hydrodynamical methods have historically been inferior in this regard compared to Eulerian or pseudo-Lagrangian methods. This work aims to remedy this discrepancy. We present the first efforts to implement a shockfinder algorithm with shock surface reconstruction for meshless finite mass (MFM) hydrodynamic schemes. We show its accuracy compared to analytic predictions and a legacy smoothed particle hydrodynamics (SPH)- based shock-finding method. We apply this new shock-finding method to simulations of cosmic structure formation to obtain improved predictions for shock energy dissipation and cosmic ray (CR) acceleration.

title: On The Scaling Relations Between Black Holes And The Galaxy/Bulge Mass And Their Connections With The Black Hole Occupation Fraction
summary: We investigate the black hole (BH)--host galaxy scaling relations predicted by the semianalytic model \texttt{FEGA25}, focusing on their dependence on BH mass threshold, galaxy morphology, and redshift, and on their connection with the BH occupation fraction (BHOF). Using the YS200 cosmological simulation as our reference volume, we study the $M_{\rm BH}$--$M_{\star}$ and $M_{\rm BH}$--$M_{\rm bulge}$ relations for different BH mass selections and compare their redshift evolution with the hydrodynamical zoom-in simulation \texttt{NewCluster}. We find that BH mass cuts primarily affect the low-mass regime, while the selected relations progressively converge toward the intrinsic no-cut relations at higher host masses. The $M_{\rm BH}$--$M_{\star}$ relation also depends systematically on galaxy morphology, with increasingly bulge-dominated systems preferentially occupying higher stellar masses. Over $z=0$--$3$, FEGA25 shows no clear systematic evolution of either scaling relation, consistent with a broadly preserved statistical connection between BH and host-galaxy growth. NewCluster shows no clear monotonic evolution either, although it exhibits larger scatter, particularly toward high host masses. We further show that BHOF and BH--host scaling relations encode complementary information. A low BHOF generally corresponds to a stronger selection-induced offset, but the mapping is not unique: substantially different occupation fractions can yield similar median scaling relations, and at fixed BHOF the bias depends on the host property and underlying BH mass distribution. At $z=0$, \texttt{FEGA25} is consistent with available observational constraints for both stellar- and bulge-mass relations, while predicting increased scatter and bending toward lower host masses.

title: Infrared spectroscopy of the longest-period Galactic Mira variables from Palomar Gattini-IR: Identification of a candidate thermally pulsing Super-Asymptotic Giant Branch star
summary: The population of extremely long-period Mira variables in the Milky Way remains poorly characterized. Their rarity and heavy circumstellar obscuration have precluded systematic studies in optical surveys, yet they are expected to trace the most massive stars evolving through the Asymptotic Giant Branch (AGB). We present IRTF/SpeX spectroscopy of the longest-period ($P\gtrsim1000$ d) Galactic Mira variables identified with the Palomar Gattini-IR survey. Twelve of thirteen targets exhibit characteristics consistent with massive O-rich AGB stars. In contrast, one peculiar source IRAS 19552+3142 exhibits i) a large-amplitude ($ΔJ\gtrsim2$ mag) pulsations with $P\approx1060$ d, ii) strong C$_2$ and CO molecular bands indicating C/O$\gtrsim1$, and iii) SiC emission at $\approx11.3\,μ$m in archival mid-infrared spectra. Its spectroscopically confirmed chemistry makes it the longest period C-rich Galactic Mira variable known; together with the rarity of similar objects, this source is difficult to reconcile with standard massive AGB evolution where hot-bottom burning maintains an O-rich surface composition. Instead, its properties may be explained by super-AGB evolution where dredge-out episodes produce a C-rich surface and circumstellar material. Its high luminosity ($M_{[4.5]}\lesssim-10$ mag), red color ($[3.6] - [4.5]\gtrsim2.0$ mag), and high mass-loss rate ($\gtrsim 10^{-4} \mathrm{M_\odot yr^{-1}}$) resemble extreme AGB star progenitors of intermediate-luminosity red transients in nearby galaxies and a known chemically peculiar super-AGB star candidate in the Small Magellanic Cloud. IRAS 19552+3142 may thus provide a rare look at a Galactic super-AGB star in the thermally pulsing phase. Our results motivate improved theoretical predictions and long-baseline infrared searches for these short-lived, dust-enshrouded endpoints of stellar evolution.

title: Chemodynamical Study and Evidence for Hot Compact Companions to Blue Straggler Stars in Berkeley 31
summary: We present a detailed study of the open cluster Berkeley 31 using Gaia DR3 astrometry, Gaia-ESO Survey DR5.1 spectroscopy, and multi-wavelength photometry. We identify 329 probable cluster members from their proper motions and trigonometric parallaxes and use them to examine the cluster's fundamental parameters, stellar populations, and Galactic orbit. The cluster is located at a distance of $6024 \pm 181$ pc, with a color excess of $E(B-V)=0.148 \pm 0.047$ mag, and has a mean metallicity of [Fe/H] $=-0.36 \pm 0.04$ dex and $\langle [α/{\rm Fe}] \rangle=0.21 \pm 0.04$ dex. Isochrone fitting gives an age of $3.7 \pm 0.2$ Gyr, consistent with the independent chemical-clock estimate of $3.72 \pm 1.42$ Gyr. The systemic radial velocity is $57.89 \pm 0.08$ km s$^{-1}$. We find that about 38% of the MS stars are unresolved binary candidates with $q \gtrsim 0.5$. We identify 62 BSSs and 2 YSS candidates, including 48 BSSs and both YSSs not previously reported in the literature. We constructed multi-wavelength SEDs for these stars, including Swift/UVOT data for 28 BSSs. Two BSSs show clear ultraviolet excesses and are consistent with compact hot companions, one with a hot WD and the other with a pre-ELM WD. The present orbital parameters give a guiding radius of $12.29 \pm 0.29$ kpc and an eccentricity of $0.11 \pm 0.01$. Comparison with the estimated chemical birth radius indicates a moderate outward shift of the guiding center, with the present orbital position also contributing to the radial displacement. These results consistently describe Berkeley 31 as an intermediate-age, metal-poor outer-disk cluster and place its stellar populations in the context of its Galactic dynamical history.

title: Probing Multi-formation Channels of Dark Matter-Deficient Galaxies in a Simulated Universe
summary: We investigate the formation and evolution of dark matter-deficient galaxies (DMDGs) using the IllustrisTNG100 cosmological hydrodynamical simulation. We define DMDGs as systems with a dark matter-to-stellar mass ratio below unity, and find two formation channels. In the first, galaxies that initially form within massive dark matter halos lose the majority of their dark matter and transition into DMDGs (acquired DMDGs). In the second, galaxies form with little or no dark matter from the beginning (inborn DMDGs). The two populations show distinct physical properties. Acquired DMDGs exhibit significant temporal variations in mass content, size, and kinematics, whereas inborn DMDGs show mild evolution. The former population tends to form closer to their nearest neighbor galaxies in large-scale overdense regions than the latter population does. We find that most stars in the inborn DMDGs form in situ. Their precursor gas is already metal-enriched and associated with other galaxies before formation. Tidal interactions and filamentary gas flows may contribute to the assembly of compact gas clumps, suggesting multiple formation pathways for inborn DMDGs. Our findings support the idea that there are at least two distinct channels to make galaxies dark matter deficient, which is important for understanding the formation mechanisms of these extreme systems.

title: The $δ$ Scuti instability strip and period-luminosity relation as seen by TESS and Gaia DR3
summary: We present an asteroseismic survey of 1,526,218 A- and F-type stars in and around the $δ$ Scuti instability strip using TESS 10-minute cadence data, which resolve the full $δ$ Scuti pulsation spectra across nearly the entire sky. We derive homogeneous stellar parameters from Gaia DR3 parallaxes and archival photometry, with temperatures that agree with interferometry to within ~300 K. A Positive--Unlabelled classifier identifies 156,706 $δ$ Scuti pulsators, which on average rotate significantly faster than non-variable A-type stars. Within the instability strip in the $T_{eff}$--$\log L$ plane, the pulsator fraction peaks at 30% over the full sample and rises to 80% in the brightest magnitude bins. Detection sensitivity therefore accounts for much, but not all, of the apparent impurity of the strip. Our period--luminosity relation agrees with previous determinations, and we recast it as a scale-invariant period--density relation that connects directly to the pulsation constant. We find that the secondary ridge in these relations is probably a combination of several overtone modes. The $δ$ Scuti stars closest to the fundamental ridge have systematically lower rotational velocities and occupy a distinct region of the instability strip. Finally, a cross-match with a Gaia catalog of open clusters reveals a correlation between the mean pulsation frequency of $δ$ Scuti stars and cluster age, suggesting a new ensemble asteroseismic age indicator for young stellar populations.

title: The unresolved high-mass frontier of the black hole Fundamental Plane
summary: Accreting black holes follow a Fundamental Plane (FP) linking radio and X-ray luminosities to black hole mass, but whether this relation changes in the ultramassive regime, above $\sim10^{10}\,\Msun$, remains unresolved. Brightest cluster galaxies (BCGs) provide the most direct access to this regime, although earlier claims of enhanced radio emission relied largely on heterogeneous nuclear measurements and black hole masses inferred from host-galaxy proxies. We recalibrate the forward FP using galaxies with direct dynamical mass measurements and reassess the evidence for a high-mass radio excess using the available BCG data. We find that the archival proxy-mass sample cannot uniquely establish such an excess because the inferred signal remains sensitive to the mass calibration and radio-selection properties of the sample. Using mock observing programs, we further show that the predictive width measured from existing observations makes a high-mass transition difficult to both detect and localize with present samples. The existing data therefore provide no compelling evidence for a distinct high-mass branch of the FP. Resolving this question will require a substantially larger, uniformly selected sample of galaxies with direct black hole masses and matched, preferably quasi-simultaneous, nuclear radio and X-ray measurements. A focused pilot survey of several dozen direct-mass systems would provide a practical first step toward establishing whether the required precision is achievable.

title: An Empirically Calibrated [C II] Luminosity-Halo Mass Relation for Line Intensity Mapping
summary: Millimeter-wave line intensity mapping aims to observe the high-redshift universe through the 158 $μ$m fine-structure line of [C II], the brightest far-infrared line of star-forming galaxies. Whether a [C II] experiment at $z>4$ measures the clustering of large-scale structure, which carries rich cosmological information, rather than the shot noise of the emitters depends on the amplitude and the shape of the [C II] power spectrum. Forecasts often build the power spectrum from a halo mass--luminosity relation, $L(M_h)$, chained from scaling relations measured in other regimes or read off simulations, without a quantified uncertainty. We instead calibrate a double power-law $L(M_h,z)$ on [C II] data alone: the mean [C II] intensity from tomographic cross-correlation at $0.4<z<4.2$ and the luminosity-function measurements and limits at $z\simeq0$ and $4.3\lesssim z\lesssim8$. The four parameters of the double power law are fitted at $z=4.5$ and $5.5$ separately, with no assumption about their evolution, and then jointly across $0<z<7$, and we examine how the uncertainty depends on the modeling assumptions. The shape of the power spectrum is settled by the existing data. The clustering peak stands a factor of $45\,(23$-$93)$ and $64\,(38$-$112)$ above the shot-noise floor at $z=4.5$ and $5.5$, and the two cross at $k_c\simeq0.37$ and $0.44\,h$Mpc$^{-1}$. The amplitude is known less well, the clustering power to $0.5-0.6$ dex and the shot noise to $0.7-0.9$ dex. The results show that the signal comes from halos accessible by current galaxy surveys, those that host the Lyman-break galaxies and Ly$α$ emitters at these redshifts. The luminosity-weighted bias is relatively high, with values of $4-5$.

title: Robust statistical significance for Gravitational Wave inference
summary: The field of gravitational-wave data analysis heavily relies on Bayes factors to make statements about astrophysical effects in events detected by the LIGO-Virgo-KAGRA collaboration. This is true on an event level, for example when discussing the potential detection of precession or eccentricity, as well as on a population level. For the latter, perhaps the main limiting factor is the reliance on the output from event-level nested sampling analyses, which is known to introduce growing uncertainties and biases as the number of detections increases. In both cases, while Bayes factors are useful when comparing different models, because the underlying distribution of Bayes factors in noise is unknown, it is often not possible to use them to make quantifiable statistical statements. Their statistical meaning is also questionable in the at least $20\%$ of gravitational-wave events that contain transient noise artifacts. This paper shows that it is possible to use evidence networks, which can infer Bayes factors after learning the distinguishability between datasets, to solve all of the aforementioned problems. By being able to calculate up to $10^5$ Bayes factors per second, we can construct background distributions of Bayes factors under different signal assumptions to estimate significance. We show that the high precision achieved allows us to scale the results from up to $10^4$ events with no discernable bias on population-level quantities, while laying the foundations for a likelihood-free method that does not rely on the assumption of Gaussian and stationary noise.

title: Dwarf Galaxy Reticulum II's MeerKAT L-Band Observation: Constraining WIMP Dark Matter
summary: The nature of dark matter remains one of the most profound open questions in modern physics, with weakly interacting massive particles (WIMPs) among the leading candidates proposed to account for the observed anomalies across cosmic scales. If WIMPs annihilate or decay in the dense dark matter haloes of nearby galaxies, the resulting high-energy electrons/positrons can produce synchrotron radiation in the presence of ambient magnetic fields, yielding a potentially detectable radio signature. Dwarf spheroidal galaxies are particularly promising targets for indirect dark matter searches due to their high mass-to-light ratios and low astrophysical foreground contamination. While radio observations have been widely used to constrain WIMP properties in these systems, the resulting limits remain highly sensitive to poorly constrained magnetic field assumptions. Here we utilize L-band ($1.3$--$1.5$ GHz) observations from the MeerKAT array directed towards dwarf galaxy Reticulum II and measure the surface brightness profile across the dwarf galaxy. Combining these measurements with theoretical models of WIMP annihilation and yield 95% confidence level upper limits on the WIMP annihilation cross-section $\langleσv\rangle \lesssim 10^{-26}$ cm$^3$ s$^{-1}$ for masses $m_χ\sim 10$-$200$ GeV (with the assumed uniform magnetic field model and diffusion constant). As next-generation radio facilities such as the Square Kilometre Array come online, robust characterisation of magnetic environments in dwarf galaxies will be essential to fully exploit their sensitivity to the particle nature of dark matter.

title: Towards an Astronomical Use of New-Generation Geodetic Observations
summary:
This thesis explores the astronomical use of observations from the VLBI Global Observing System (VGOS), a next-generation geodetic network designed to improve the precision of terrestrial and celestial reference frames and Earth orientation parameters. Although primarily conceived for geodesy, its wide frequency coverage and regular monitoring of compact active galactic nuclei (AGN) provide valuable opportunities for astrophysics.
  We develop a calibration pipeline that transforms VGOS correlator outputs into full-polarization, calibrated visibilities suitable for astronomical imaging. The procedure combines linear-to-circular polarization conversion, instrumental phase and amplitude calibration, and a new wideband global fringe-fitting algorithm that accounts for dispersive ionospheric effects.
